claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is governed by the degree of atomic-level chemical disorder.
Atomic-level chemical disorder modulates local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions tune electron-phonon coupling strength.
Electron-phonon coupling strength determines the superconducting transition temperature.
Changing constituent-element composition ratios can systematically vary atomic-level chemical disorder while retaining the same overall phase.
Local atomic-level disorder induces variations in lattice distortion.
Changes in chemical disorder modify the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Disorder-induced changes in electron-phonon coupling and electronic density of states affect Cooper-pair formation.
A moderate increase in chemical disorder enhances electron-phonon interactions.
Excessive disorder introduces scattering that degrades superconductivity.
Increasing atomic-level disorder should increase electron-phonon coupling strength and elevate Tc relative to the baseline until an optimum is reached.
Further disorder beyond the optimum may reduce Tc through enhanced scattering.
Near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys produce minimal chemical disorder.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase metallic high-entropy alloys composed of non-magnetic elements.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when phase separation, disorder-induced amorphization, or alternative pairing mechanisms occur.

contradictions.description: The initial alloy is described as nominally random, while the near-equiatomic baseline is said to have minimal chemical disorder and departures from it are assumed to increase disorder. The hypothesis does not define a disorder metric that reconciles nominal randomness with the claim that the near-equiatomic state is minimally disordered.
